html:
The first coffeehouses in Istanbul opened in 1555, according to an Ottoman chronicler, started by two men from Aleppo and Damascus. Within a few decades there were hundreds, and they became the city's main places for talk, games and news.

Coffee had come from Yemen, where coffee drinking began among Sufis, by way of Mecca and Cairo. In Istanbul men gathered to drink it, play chess and backgammon, hear storytellers and poets and argue about politics. Some called the coffeehouses "schools of knowledge". The coffee was ground fine and boiled in a small pot, the style now called Turkish coffee.

Religious scholars attacked the drink, and sultans feared the gossip and plotting. Murad IV closed the coffeehouses in 1633 and punished drinkers harshly, but they came back. Through Ottoman contacts the habit spread to Europe, with coffeehouses opening in Venice, London and Paris in the 17th century, and after the siege of Vienna in 1683 legend gives Vienna its first café. Beans came through the Mocha trade in Yemen, then part of the Ottoman Empire.
